description: Editorial description of the on-screen teaching sequence; not spoken narration. The soundtrack is music.

segments.text: A Transformer builds representations by allowing positions in a sequence to exchange information through attention.
The sentence about a robot dropping a glass motivates the need to use context when interpreting a token.
Tokens are converted to vectors, and information about their positions is added or otherwise supplied.
Attention assigns weights to other positions and mixes their value vectors to form context-dependent representations.
A bidirectional example can use words on both sides. Causal attention can use only the current and earlier positions.
Multiple attention heads can learn different patterns of interaction.
A Transformer block combines attention with a position-wise feed-forward network, normalization and residual connections.
Stacking blocks repeatedly refines the token representations.
An output head maps representations to task-specific predictions.
Encoder-style models commonly use bidirectional context. Decoder-style language models commonly use causal attention.
Encoder–decoder models add attention from decoder states to encoder outputs, supporting tasks such as translation.
Known training positions can be processed in parallel with a mask. Autoregressive generation still extends the sequence one token at a time.
The module develops a small character-level language model so that the full computation is inspectable.
Modern language models may use variants such as rotary positions, RMSNorm or different feed-forward designs; they are not all present in this teaching model.
Transformers can also operate on image patches and other kinds of tokenized input.
The following lessons unpack input preparation, attention, blocks, assembly and training in detail.
